newsitem.title: USA: Jury deliberations resume in du Pont murder trial.
newsitem.headline: Jury deliberations resume in du Pont murder trial.

text.p: Jurors resumed deliberations on Wednesday in the trial of chemicals heir John du Pont, accused of killing Olympic champion wrestler David Schultz.

The six men and six women spent slightly less than three hours considering their verdict on Tuesday. Du Pont, 58, could be convicted of first degree or third degree murder or voluntary manslaughter in the Jan. 26, 1996 slaying of Schultz, who lived on du Pont's suburban Philadelphia estate and coached at a wrestling training facility there.

Du Pont's attorney, in closing arguments on Tuesday, asked the jury to find him not guilty by reason of insanity, saying he suffered from paranoid schitzophrenia that rendered him incapable of knowing his actions were wrong.
Prosecutors contended that du Pont acted out of anger and arrogance after his relationship with Schutlz grew strained. They said du Pont was aware of what he was doing.
The jury can find du Pont guilty, not guilty, not guilty by reason of insanity, or guilty but mentally ill on any of the three homicide counts.

An alternate juror, excused after Court of Common Pleas Judge Patricia Jenkins gave final instructions on Tuesday, told reporters he thought du Pont should be found guilty but mentally ill. He said he thought du Pont used his unkempt appearance in court as a ploy.

"I think he's guilty. I think he is mentally ill but I think he knew what he was doing at the time. He knew he was killing a man and he knew that it was wrong," Albert Allen, 45, told reporters in a telephone conference call.
Throughout the 13 days of testimony, du Pont came to court with shaggy hair and an untrimmed beard, wearing sweat clothes with the logo of his Foxcatcher wrestling team.
"If he came in dressed the way a man of his means can dress and be groomed it would have sat better with me and maybe some of the others," Allen said.
A verdict of guilty but mentally ill would carry the same maximum penalties as a regular guilty verdict but allow for du Pont to be treated before serving out the remainder of his sentence in prison.

Allen said he did not think du Pont's illness prevented him from knowing right from wrong -- a key criterion for legal insanity. "The guy was crazy but not insane," he said, adding that the deciding factors included du Pont's decision to carry a larger than customary .44 calibre pistol when he drove to Schultz's house and his firing of a third shot into Schultz's prone body.
